mixture-of-experts-moe.idea: Instead of sending every input through a single large feed-forward network, sparse routing activates only a few specialized expert sub-networks per token via a top-k gating mechanism.
mixture-of-experts-moe.why: Dense layers waste capacity on inputs that do not need all parameters. Sparse expert routing scales model capacity while keeping per-token computation manageable.
mixture-of-experts-moe.example: Imagine a team that routes each support ticket to the specialist who handles that category, so no single agent must master every domain.

rotary-positional-embeddings-rope.idea: Token positions are encoded by rotating query and key vectors in paired dimensions using orthogonal rotation matrices, making relative distance emerge naturally from the dot product.
rotary-positional-embeddings-rope.why: Fixed sinusoidal embeddings struggle when sequences grow beyond the lengths seen during training. Rotary embeddings allow attention to extrapolate to longer contexts more gracefully.
rotary-positional-embeddings-rope.example: Imagine a team that labels each desk with a compass heading; the relative angle between adjacent desks reveals their spatial relationship without absolute coordinates.

residual-connections-resnet.idea: Identity skip connections let each layer learn a residual correction on top of its input rather than an entirely new mapping, easing gradient flow through deep stacks.
residual-connections-resnet.why: Very deep networks suffer from vanishing gradients and degradation, where added layers paradoxically increase training error. Skip connections stabilize learning by providing gradient shortcuts.
residual-connections-resnet.example: Imagine a team that reviews a draft document where each editor marks only the changes, keeping the original text intact so no revision can make the document worse than the prior version.

sliding-window-and-longformer-attention.idea: Each token attends only to a fixed-size local window of neighbors plus a few designated global anchor tokens, replacing the full quadratic attention matrix with sparse bands.
sliding-window-and-longformer-attention.why: Full self-attention over very long documents is prohibitively expensive. Sliding windows with dilated and global tokens preserve relevant long-range context at a fraction of the cost.
sliding-window-and-longformer-attention.example: Imagine a team that assigns each member to coordinate with nearby seats but also connects a few leads who can relay information across the entire room.

grouped-query-attention-gqa.idea: Multiple query heads share a smaller set of key-value heads, reducing the memory bandwidth required to load cached key-value tensors during generation.
grouped-query-attention-gqa.why: Standard multi-head attention duplicates key-value projections for every query head, wasting memory bandwidth at inference. Grouping preserves quality while cutting memory transfers.
grouped-query-attention-gqa.example: Imagine a team that shares one reference binder among several analysts instead of photocopying it for each person, cutting supply costs without losing access to the information.

lora-low-rank-adaptation.idea: Pre-trained weights stay frozen while small trainable rank-decomposition matrix pairs are injected into attention and MLP layers, drastically reducing the parameter count updated during fine-tuning.
lora-low-rank-adaptation.why: Full fine-tuning of large models demands enormous memory and storage for separate weight copies. Low-rank adapters achieve comparable task performance with a tiny fraction of trainable parameters.
lora-low-rank-adaptation.example: Imagine a team that customizes a shared office template by attaching small sticky-note overlays rather than rewriting the entire manual for each department.

qlora-quantized-fine-tuning.idea: Combines low-rank adaptation with aggressive weight quantization so that a very large frozen model fits in memory on limited hardware while remaining fine-tunable through small adapters.
qlora-quantized-fine-tuning.why: Even with parameter-efficient methods, loading the base model consumes most available memory. Quantizing the frozen weights reclaims that space so adapters can still be trained.
qlora-quantized-fine-tuning.example: Imagine a team that compresses a huge reference library into summary cards so the entire collection fits on a single shelf, then adds detailed margin notes only where needed.

direct-preference-optimization-dpo.idea: Trains a language model directly on pairs of preferred and rejected outputs using a classification-style loss, removing the need for a separate reward model or reinforcement learning loop.
direct-preference-optimization-dpo.why: Reward-model-based alignment pipelines add engineering complexity, instability, and extra compute. A direct preference loss simplifies the pipeline while producing comparable alignment quality.
direct-preference-optimization-dpo.example: Imagine a team that asks editors to pick the better of paired drafts and uses those choices directly to train a writing assistant, skipping the step of scoring every possible draft.

rlhf-proximal-policy-optimization.idea: A reward model trained on human comparison judgments provides a scalar signal that guides policy gradient updates to align language model outputs with human intentions.
rlhf-proximal-policy-optimization.why: Supervised fine-tuning on curated examples teaches style but not preferences among open-ended responses. Reinforcement signals from human comparisons steer the model toward broadly preferred behavior.
rlhf-proximal-policy-optimization.example: Imagine a team that asks taste-testers to rank recipe variations, then uses those rankings to guide a chef toward dishes that satisfy the widest palate.

constitutional-ai-and-rlaif.idea: A set of natural-language principles forms a constitution that the model uses to self-critique and revise its own outputs, generating synthetic preference pairs for training without human labeling.
constitutional-ai-and-rlaif.why: Collecting human feedback is slow and expensive at scale. Self-critique loops guided by explicit principles can produce alignment data more rapidly while remaining transparent.
constitutional-ai-and-rlaif.example: Imagine a team that posts a code-of-conduct checklist on the wall and asks each writer to self-edit against it before submitting, reducing the need for external reviewers.

kahneman-tversky-optimization-kto.idea: Applies prospect theory from behavioral economics to model alignment, weighting losses from bad outputs more heavily than equivalent gains from good outputs using unpaired binary feedback.
kahneman-tversky-optimization-kto.why: Paired preference data is hard to collect at scale. Treating each output independently as acceptable or unacceptable simplifies data collection while capturing asymmetric human value sensitivity.
kahneman-tversky-optimization-kto.example: Imagine a team that rates each customer service reply as either helpful or unhelpful, then weighs unhelpful replies more heavily when retraining the response guide.

prompt-tuning-and-prefix-tuning.idea: All pre-trained weights remain frozen while a small set of continuous learnable virtual token embeddings is prepended to the input or injected into key-value layers to steer model behavior.
prompt-tuning-and-prefix-tuning.why: Full fine-tuning demands separate weight copies per task. Learning only a handful of soft prompt parameters enables multi-task serving from a single shared base model.
prompt-tuning-and-prefix-tuning.example: Imagine a team that keeps the employee handbook untouched but adds a custom cover page for each department that frames how staff should interpret the same rules.

flashattention-tiling-kernel.idea: Restructures the attention computation into memory-aware tiles that shuttle data between fast on-chip memory and slower main memory, avoiding materialization of the full attention matrix.
flashattention-tiling-kernel.why: Standard attention kernels are bottlenecked by memory reads and writes, not raw arithmetic. Tiling the softmax computation to stay on-chip dramatically improves throughput and cuts memory use.
flashattention-tiling-kernel.example: Imagine a team that processes a large spreadsheet by loading only a few rows at a time into a fast desktop calculator rather than printing the entire sheet and scanning it repeatedly.

kv-caching-autoregressive-decoding.idea: During token-by-token generation, previously computed key and value tensors are cached so each new token only needs to compute its own projections and attend to the stored history.
kv-caching-autoregressive-decoding.why: Without caching, every generated token would recompute attention over the entire preceding sequence, making generation quadratically expensive. Caching reduces each step to a single new row of work.
kv-caching-autoregressive-decoding.example: Imagine a team that keeps meeting minutes in a shared notebook so each new attendee reads the notes instead of replaying the entire discussion from scratch.

pagedattention-virtual-memory.idea: Borrows virtual memory paging concepts from operating systems to manage the key-value cache in non-contiguous memory blocks, eliminating fragmentation waste during concurrent request serving.
pagedattention-virtual-memory.why: Pre-allocating contiguous memory per request wastes space when sequence lengths vary widely. Paging allows flexible, on-demand allocation that raises overall serving throughput.
pagedattention-virtual-memory.example: Imagine a team that stores archive boxes on whichever shelf has space rather than reserving a full row per project, freeing up room for more active projects.

speculative-decoding-draft-models.idea: A smaller, faster draft model generates several candidate tokens in parallel, and the larger target model verifies them in a single forward pass, accepting correct guesses and rejecting wrong tokens.
speculative-decoding-draft-models.why: Large model inference is bottlenecked by memory bandwidth rather than computation. Batching verification of cheap speculative tokens amortizes that bandwidth cost over multiple accepted tokens.
speculative-decoding-draft-models.example: Imagine a team that has a junior assistant draft a paragraph and a senior editor reviews it in a single pass, keeping correct sentences and rewriting only the flawed parts.

awq-activation-aware-quantization.idea: Compresses model weights to low-bit precision by identifying the salient weight channels that correspond to high-magnitude activations and protecting them with per-channel scaling before quantization.
awq-activation-aware-quantization.why: Uniform quantization degrades model quality by rounding critical weights. Protecting activation-sensitive channels preserves output accuracy while still achieving substantial compression.
awq-activation-aware-quantization.example: Imagine a team that rounds most budget line items to coarse figures but keeps the high-impact items at exact dollar amounts to maintain overall fiscal accuracy.

gptq-post-training-quantization.idea: Uses second-order error compensation to quantize each weight column sequentially, redistributing rounding error to remaining unquantized columns so that overall layer output stays close to the original.
gptq-post-training-quantization.why: Naive rounding of weights accumulates error rapidly across a large model. Layer-wise curvature-guided compensation keeps total output deviation small even at aggressive compression levels.
gptq-post-training-quantization.example: Imagine a team that adjusts each ingredient in a recipe sequentially, tweaking subsequent ingredients to compensate so the final dish tastes like the original.

continuous-batching-orca.idea: Schedules requests at the token-iteration level rather than the request level, immediately filling empty batch slots when any request finishes instead of waiting for the entire batch to complete.
continuous-batching-orca.why: Static batching wastes compute when short requests finish early but must wait for long ones. Continuous insertion keeps hardware utilization high across variable-length workloads.
continuous-batching-orca.example: Imagine a team that fills empty chairs at a group workshop the moment a participant leaves, rather than waiting for the whole session to end before seating newcomers.

beam-search-and-top-p-sampling.idea: Nucleus sampling dynamically selects from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold, balancing diversity and coherence during text generation.
beam-search-and-top-p-sampling.why: Greedy or fixed-k sampling either produces repetitive text or includes low-probability noise. A dynamic probability threshold adapts to each step's confidence distribution naturally.
beam-search-and-top-p-sampling.example: Imagine a team that brainstorms ideas by considering only the suggestions that collectively cover most of the group's confidence, discarding fringe proposals automatically.

dense-retrieval-bi-encoders.idea: Twin neural encoders map queries and documents into a shared continuous embedding space so that relevance reduces to a fast nearest-neighbor vector similarity search.
dense-retrieval-bi-encoders.why: Keyword matching misses semantically similar passages that use different wording. Dense embeddings capture meaning rather than surface tokens, improving recall on paraphrased content.
dense-retrieval-bi-encoders.example: Imagine a team that summarizes each report into a fingerprint code, then finds related reports by comparing fingerprints rather than scanning every page for shared keywords.

cross-encoder-reranking.idea: Feeds a query-document pair jointly through full self-attention layers, capturing deep token-level interactions that bi-encoder similarity scores miss, to rerank a shortlist of retrieval candidates.
cross-encoder-reranking.why: Bi-encoders encode query and document independently, limiting interaction to a single similarity score. Joint encoding enables fine-grained relevance distinctions among top candidates.
cross-encoder-reranking.example: Imagine a team that first filters resumes by keyword match, then has a senior reviewer read each shortlisted resume alongside the job description for a nuanced ranking.

hierarchical-navigable-small-world-hnsw.idea: Builds a multi-layer proximity graph where upper layers contain long-range skip connections and lower layers hold dense local edges, enabling greedy nearest-neighbor search in logarithmic time.
hierarchical-navigable-small-world-hnsw.why: Exhaustive search through millions of high-dimensional vectors is too slow for real-time applications. The hierarchical graph structure provides sub-millisecond approximate lookups with high recall.
hierarchical-navigable-small-world-hnsw.example: Imagine a team that organizes a library using an express index of broad categories on the top floor and progressively more detailed catalogs on each lower floor to find any book quickly.

graphrag-knowledge-graph-retrieval.idea: Extracts entity-relationship graphs and community summaries from document collections so that retrieval can traverse structured connections rather than relying solely on vector similarity.
graphrag-knowledge-graph-retrieval.why: Flat vector search struggles to synthesize answers that require connecting facts scattered across many separate passages. Graph traversal gathers related entities along explicit relationship edges.
graphrag-knowledge-graph-retrieval.example: Imagine a team that builds an org chart from scattered meeting notes, then answers questions about reporting chains by following the chart rather than re-reading every note.

hypothetical-document-embeddings-hyde.idea: An instruction-tuned language model generates a hypothetical answer document for a user query, and that synthetic document is embedded and used to retrieve real documents by vector similarity.
hypothetical-document-embeddings-hyde.why: Queries are typically short and lack the vocabulary overlap that dense retrievers rely on. A generated pseudo-document bridges the lexical gap between terse queries and verbose passages.
hypothetical-document-embeddings-hyde.example: Imagine a team that writes a rough draft answer to a research question first, then searches the archive for documents that sound similar to that draft.

denoising-diffusion-probabilistic-models.idea: Generates data by learning to reverse a fixed forward process that incrementally adds noise to training samples, recovering clean data from pure noise step by step through a learned denoising network.
denoising-diffusion-probabilistic-models.why: Generative adversarial approaches suffer from unstable training dynamics and mode collapse. The iterative denoising framework offers stable training with a simple reconstruction objective.
denoising-diffusion-probabilistic-models.example: Imagine a team that trains a photo restorer by gradually blurring training images and teaching the system to sharpen each stage until the original clarity is recovered.

classifier-free-guidance-cfg.idea: Steers the diffusion sampling process toward a text prompt by jointly training conditional and unconditional generation paths, then amplifying the difference between them at inference.
classifier-free-guidance-cfg.why: Classifier-based guidance requires training a separate classifier on noisy inputs. Dropping the classifier simplifies the pipeline and allows more flexible prompt-following behavior.
classifier-free-guidance-cfg.example: Imagine a team that drafts paired versions of a poster, with and without a creative brief, then exaggerates the differences to make the final poster strongly reflect that brief.

latent-diffusion-models-stable-diffusion.idea: Moves the iterative diffusion and denoising process from high-dimensional pixel space into the compressed latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder, dramatically reducing computational cost.
latent-diffusion-models-stable-diffusion.why: Running diffusion directly on full-resolution images consumes enormous compute and memory. Operating in a compact latent space preserves visual quality while making generation feasible.
latent-diffusion-models-stable-diffusion.example: Imagine a team that sketches thumbnails to iterate on composition quickly, then expands the chosen thumbnail into a full-size painting only at the final step.

variational-autoencoders-vae.idea: Encodes inputs into a smooth continuous latent distribution using the reparameterization trick, enabling both faithful reconstruction and generation of new samples by sampling from that distribution.
variational-autoencoders-vae.why: Standard autoencoders learn fragmented latent spaces with gaps that produce nonsensical outputs when sampled. Enforcing a smooth prior ensures meaningful interpolation and generation.
variational-autoencoders-vae.example: Imagine a team that catalogs furniture designs on a smooth style spectrum so that picking any point on the spectrum produces a coherent new design rather than a random collage.

vector-quantized-vae-vqvae.idea: Replaces the continuous latent space of a standard autoencoder with a discrete codebook, snapping each encoded vector to its nearest codebook entry to learn compact symbolic representations.
vector-quantized-vae-vqvae.why: Continuous latent spaces can suffer from posterior collapse in powerful decoders. Discrete codes force the encoder to use the bottleneck meaningfully and enable autoregressive generation over tokens.
vector-quantized-vae-vqvae.example: Imagine a team that compresses voice recordings into sequences of short standard phoneme codes, then reconstructs speech by playing back the corresponding code entries in order.

adamw-decoupled-weight-decay.idea: Separates weight decay from the adaptive gradient update so that regularization strength remains consistent regardless of the per-parameter learning rate scaling applied by the optimizer.
adamw-decoupled-weight-decay.why: When weight decay is coupled with adaptive momentum, parameters with large gradients receive disproportionately weak regularization. Decoupling ensures uniform shrinkage across all weights.
adamw-decoupled-weight-decay.example: Imagine a team that applies a flat overhead fee to every department rather than folding it into variable performance bonuses, keeping the administrative charge predictable.

rms-normalization-and-layer-norm.idea: Normalizes activations by their root mean square alone, skipping the mean-centering step used in standard layer normalization, yielding a simpler and computationally cheaper operation.
rms-normalization-and-layer-norm.why: Mean centering adds extra computation and memory accesses with minimal quality benefit in deep transformer stacks. Removing it speeds up each normalization step without degrading model accuracy.
rms-normalization-and-layer-norm.example: Imagine a team that calibrates instruments by scaling readings to a standard magnitude without first subtracting the average, saving a step while achieving equivalent precision.

cosine-annealing-warmup-schedules.idea: Starts training with a low learning rate that linearly ramps up during a warmup phase, then smoothly decays following a cosine curve toward zero over the remaining training steps.
cosine-annealing-warmup-schedules.why: Large learning rates at initialization can destabilize randomly initialized parameters. Gradual warmup lets the optimizer settle before the cosine decay refines convergence toward a good minimum.
cosine-annealing-warmup-schedules.example: Imagine a team that eases new employees into full workloads over their onboarding period, then gradually reduces task intensity as the project winds down.

gradient-accumulation-and-mixed-precisio.idea: Runs forward and backward passes in half-precision floating point on tensor cores while maintaining a master copy of weights in full precision, halving memory use and boosting throughput.
gradient-accumulation-and-mixed-precisio.why: Full-precision arithmetic underutilizes modern accelerator hardware designed for half-precision tensor operations. Mixed precision exploits that hardware while a full-precision master copy guards against rounding drift.
gradient-accumulation-and-mixed-precisio.example: Imagine a team that drafts all internal memos in shorthand to save time but keeps a master copy in formal language to prevent meaning from drifting over successive edits.

proximal-policy-optimization-ppo.idea: An on-policy actor-critic algorithm that clips the policy gradient objective to prevent any single update from moving the policy too far from its previous version.
proximal-policy-optimization-ppo.why: Unconstrained policy gradient updates can catastrophically collapse performance by overshooting into poor policy regions. Clipping the surrogate objective enforces stable, incremental improvement.
proximal-policy-optimization-ppo.example: Imagine a team that limits each sprint's process changes to small adjustments so that no single retrospective overhaul destabilizes the workflow.

monte-carlo-tree-search-alphazero.idea: Combines a learned policy and value network with tree search, using upper confidence bounds to balance exploring new moves and exploiting promising branches during decision-making.
monte-carlo-tree-search-alphazero.why: Exhaustive search of game trees is computationally infeasible for complex domains. Neural-guided tree search focuses computation on the most promising branches, reaching strong play efficiently.
monte-carlo-tree-search-alphazero.example: Imagine a team that plans a marketing campaign by sketching several strategy branches, estimating each branch's potential, and expanding only the top contenders in detail.

deep-q-networks-dqn-experience-replay.idea: Stores past transitions in a replay buffer and samples mini-batches randomly for training, breaking temporal correlations that destabilize action-value function approximation with neural networks.
deep-q-networks-dqn-experience-replay.why: Training on consecutive experiences causes the network to overfit to recent states and forget earlier lessons. Random replay decorrelates samples and stabilizes learning across diverse situations.
deep-q-networks-dqn-experience-replay.example: Imagine a team that reviews a shuffled collection of past project post-mortems during training sessions rather than only discussing the most recent project.

clip-contrastive-language-image-pretrain.idea: Trains paired image and text encoders on web-scale image-caption data using a contrastive loss that pulls matching pairs together and pushes non-matching pairs apart in a shared embedding space.
clip-contrastive-language-image-pretrain.why: Traditional vision models require task-specific labeled datasets for each new classification problem. Contrastive language-image training enables flexible recognition of unseen categories guided by natural language descriptions.
clip-contrastive-language-image-pretrain.example: Imagine a team that teaches an archivist to match photographs with their captions so well that the archivist can later sort unseen photos into any described category.

llava-visual-instruction-tuning.idea: Bridges a pre-trained vision encoder and a language model decoder through a projection layer, enabling the combined system to follow visual instructions and answer questions about images.
llava-visual-instruction-tuning.why: Standalone language models cannot perceive visual content, and standalone vision models lack conversational reasoning. Connecting them through a learned projection yields a unified visual dialogue system.
llava-visual-instruction-tuning.example: Imagine a team that pairs a skilled photographer with a writer through a translator, so the writer can describe and discuss any photograph the photographer shares.

neural-radiance-fields-nerf.idea: Represents a scene as a continuous volumetric function that maps spatial coordinates and viewing direction to color and density, enabling photorealistic novel-view synthesis from a set of posed images.
neural-radiance-fields-nerf.why: Traditional rendering pipelines require explicit geometry meshes, which are expensive to create for complex real-world scenes. A neural implicit function learns the scene directly from photographs.
neural-radiance-fields-nerf.example: Imagine a team that photographs a sculpture from several angles and then generates a realistic view from any new angle without building a physical replica.

3d-gaussian-splatting.idea: Represents scenes as collections of anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives that are rasterized via differentiable tile-based splatting, enabling real-time radiance field rendering.
3d-gaussian-splatting.why: Neural implicit methods like volumetric ray marching are too slow for interactive applications. Explicit point-based primitives with fast rasterization achieve comparable visual quality at interactive frame rates.
3d-gaussian-splatting.example: Imagine a team that reconstructs a room by placing and adjusting thousands of soft colored blobs in space, then renders any viewpoint by projecting those blobs onto a screen in real time.

knowledge-distillation-teacher-student.idea: Trains a compact student model to reproduce the soft probability distributions output by a larger teacher model, transferring learned knowledge into a more deployable form.
knowledge-distillation-teacher-student.why: Large models capture rich inter-class relationships in their output distributions that hard labels alone do not convey. Distilling these soft targets into a smaller model preserves much of that knowledge.
knowledge-distillation-teacher-student.example: Imagine a team that has a senior analyst write detailed explanation memos so that a junior analyst can learn the reasoning patterns without shadowing every meeting.

word2vec-skipgram-negative-sampling.idea: Trains a shallow neural network to predict surrounding context words from a center word, producing dense vector embeddings where semantically related words cluster together in geometric space.
word2vec-skipgram-negative-sampling.why: Sparse indicator word representations cannot capture similarity or analogy relationships. Dense learned vectors encode meaning so that vector arithmetic reveals linguistic regularities.
word2vec-skipgram-negative-sampling.example: Imagine a team that assigns each product a coordinate on a map such that similar products sit close together and complementary products form consistent directional patterns.

contrastive-representation-learning-simc.idea: Learns visual representations by maximizing agreement between differently augmented views of the same image while pushing apart representations of different images in the batch.
contrastive-representation-learning-simc.why: Labeled image datasets are expensive and limited in scope. Self-supervised contrastive learning extracts transferable features from unlabeled images, reducing dependence on manual annotation.
contrastive-representation-learning-simc.example: Imagine a team that identifies documents as related by checking whether different photocopies of the same page look similar, while ensuring copies of different pages look distinct.

masked-autoencoders-mae.idea: Randomly masks a large proportion of image patches and trains an asymmetric encoder-decoder to reconstruct the missing pixels, forcing the encoder to learn meaningful visual representations.
masked-autoencoders-mae.why: Processing all patches is computationally expensive and provides little self-supervisory signal. Masking most patches accelerates training and compels the model to understand spatial structure rather than memorize textures.
masked-autoencoders-mae.example: Imagine a team that gives puzzle solvers jigsaw boards with most pieces removed, training them to infer the missing sections from context clues in the visible fragments.

chinchilla-compute-optimal-scaling-laws.idea: Compute-optimal training recommends scaling model parameters and training data in tandem rather than making models as large as possible, achieving equivalent performance with less total computation.
chinchilla-compute-optimal-scaling-laws.why: Over-parameterized models trained on insufficient data waste compute and underperform relative to their budget. Balancing model size with data volume maximizes quality per unit of computation.
chinchilla-compute-optimal-scaling-laws.example: Imagine a team that balances hiring new staff with providing adequate training materials, recognizing that a larger team without enough documentation performs worse than a well-resourced smaller team.

emergent-abilities-and-grokking.idea: Grokking describes the phenomenon where a neural network memorizes training data quickly but then, after extended further training, suddenly transitions to genuine generalization on held-out inputs.
emergent-abilities-and-grokking.why: Standard learning curves suggest that overfitting and generalization are opposing forces. Grokking reveals that prolonged optimization can reorganize internal representations into generalizable circuits long after memorization.
emergent-abilities-and-grokking.example: Imagine a team that memorizes safety procedures by rote for weeks, then suddenly begins applying the underlying principles flexibly to novel emergency scenarios.

mechanistic-interpretability-induction-h.idea: Reverse-engineers trained neural networks into discrete, human-interpretable computational circuits, identifying specific attention head compositions responsible for capabilities like in-context pattern matching.
mechanistic-interpretability-induction-h.why: Treating a model as an opaque black box limits trust, debugging, and safety analysis. Identifying concrete circuits enables targeted interventions and deeper understanding of model behavior.
mechanistic-interpretability-induction-h.example: Imagine a team that traces a factory's output defect back to a specific pair of machines working in sequence, rather than blaming the entire assembly line.

react-reasoning-and-acting.idea: Interleaves chain-of-thought reasoning traces with tool-use actions in an alternating loop, letting a language model plan its next step, execute it, observe the result, and reason again.
react-reasoning-and-acting.why: Pure reasoning without external grounding can hallucinate facts, while blind tool calls without planning waste steps. Alternating thought and action enables self-correcting, grounded problem solving.
react-reasoning-and-acting.example: Imagine a team that tackles a research question by first hypothesizing an answer, then searching a database, reviewing the result, and refining the hypothesis before continuing.

tree-of-thoughts-prompting.idea: Expands a single reasoning chain into a branching tree of intermediate thoughts, allowing the model to evaluate, compare, and backtrack among multiple solution paths before committing to an answer.
tree-of-thoughts-prompting.why: Linear chain-of-thought prompting commits early to a single reasoning path and cannot recover from mistakes. Tree search enables deliberate exploration and pruning of dead-end strategies.
tree-of-thoughts-prompting.example: Imagine a team that sketches several possible floor plans for an office, scores each on key criteria, and drops the weakest layouts before refining the top candidates.
